front: Which law governs a contract for a mix of goods and services?
back: The predominant-purpose test (majority): if the main purpose is the sale of goods, UCC Article 2 governs the whole contract; if services, the common law. Minority: the gravamen test applies the law fitting the disputed part.

front: What are 'goods' under UCC Article 2?
back: All things movable at the time of identification to the contract, including specially manufactured goods, unborn young of animals, growing crops and timber to be cut (UCC §§ 2-105, 2-107). Not land, services, money paid as the price, or intangibles.

front: Who is a 'merchant' under UCC § 2-104?
back: One who deals in goods of the kind, or by occupation holds itself out as having knowledge or skill peculiar to the practices or goods involved. Any business person counts for §§ 2-201(2), 2-205 and 2-207; § 2-314 needs a dealer in goods of that kind.

front: What test decides whether mutual assent exists?
back: The objective theory: what a reasonable person in the other party's position would understand from words and conduct, not secret intent (Lucy v. Zehmer).

front: Define an offer (R2d § 24).
back: A manifestation of willingness to enter a bargain, made so as to justify the offeree in understanding that its assent is invited and will conclude the bargain: commitment, definite terms, communication.

front: When is an advertisement an offer?
back: Usually it is an invitation to deal. It is an offer if clear, definite and explicit, leaving nothing open, and limiting who may accept (e.g., 'first come, first served') (Lefkowitz).

front: At an auction, who is the offeror, and what is the default?
back: The bidder makes the offer; the hammer fall is acceptance. Auctions are 'with reserve' (goods may be withdrawn) unless announced 'without reserve'; a bidder may retract before the hammer falls (UCC § 2-328).

front: List the ways an offeree's power of acceptance terminates.
back: Rejection or counteroffer (on receipt); lapse (stated or reasonable time); revocation (on receipt); death or incapacity of either party (no notice needed); destruction of the subject matter; supervening illegality.

front: Is 'Would you take $9,000?' a rejection of a $10,000 offer?
back: No. A mere inquiry or request for better terms is not a counteroffer, so the offer stays open (R2d § 39 cmt.).

front: When is a revocation effective, and what is indirect revocation?
back: On receipt by the offeree. Indirect revocation: the offeree gets reliable information that the offeror has taken definite action inconsistent with the offer (Dickinson v. Dodds; R2d § 43).

front: What makes an offer irrevocable? (four doctrines)
back: 1. Option supported by consideration (R2d § 87(1)). 2. Merchant's signed firm offer (UCC § 2-205). 3. Beginning performance of a unilateral offer (R2d § 45). 4. Foreseeable reliance before acceptance (R2d § 87(2); Drennan).

front: State the merchant's firm offer rule.
back: A merchant's signed written offer to buy or sell goods that assures it will be held open is irrevocable without consideration for the stated time or a reasonable time, not exceeding 3 months; an assurance on the offeree's form must be separately signed (UCC § 2-205).

front: What happens when an offeree begins performance of a unilateral offer?
back: An option contract arises: the offeror cannot revoke, but its duty is conditional on complete performance. Mere preparation is not enough (R2d § 45).

front: What did Drennan v. Star Paving hold?
back: A subcontractor's bid that a general contractor foreseeably relied on in its own bid is irrevocable for a reasonable time; the GC can accept and recover the cost of a substitute (now R2d § 87(2)).

front: What is the common-law mirror-image rule?
back: An acceptance must match the offer exactly; a reply adding or changing terms is a rejection and counteroffer (R2d § 59; Cal. Civ. Code § 1585). A mere request that does not condition acceptance is still an acceptance (§ 61).

front: UCC § 2-207(1): when does a reply with new terms still form a contract?
back: When it is a definite and seasonable expression of acceptance, unless acceptance is expressly made conditional on assent to the additional or different terms (clear language required: Dorton).

front: UCC § 2-207(2): when do additional terms become part of the contract?
back: Only between merchants, and only if (a) the offer does not expressly limit acceptance to its terms, (b) they do not materially alter the contract, and (c) the offeror does not object within a reasonable time. Otherwise they are proposals.

front: Give examples of material vs. non-material alterations under § 2-207.
back: Material (surprise or hardship): warranty disclaimers, unusual cancellation rights, very short complaint periods. Not material: reasonable interest on overdue invoices, reasonable complaint periods, credit terms within trade practice. Arbitration clauses: courts split.

front: How are conflicting ('different') terms in the forms handled?
back: Majority knockout rule: both conflicting terms drop out, and UCC gap fillers apply (Daitom; § 2-207 cmt. 6).

front: What is a § 2-207(3) contract?
back: Where the writings do not form a contract but both parties' conduct recognizes one, a contract exists on the terms the writings agree on plus UCC gap fillers.

front: State the mailbox rule and its exceptions.
back: Acceptance is effective on dispatch by a reasonable medium, even if lost. Revocations, rejections and counteroffers are effective on receipt. Exceptions: option acceptances (on receipt), offers requiring receipt, improper medium (on receipt if timely).

front: Offeree mails a rejection, then phones an acceptance that arrives first. Result?
back: A contract is formed. When a rejection is sent first, whichever communication arrives first controls (R2d § 40).

front: Offeree mails an acceptance, then a rejection that arrives first. Result?
back: A contract was formed on dispatch of the acceptance. But if the offeror relied on the earlier-arriving rejection, the offeree is estopped from enforcing it.

front: Seller ships nonconforming goods in response to an order for prompt shipment. Effect?
back: It is both an acceptance and a breach, unless the seller seasonably notifies the buyer that the shipment is offered only as an accommodation, which makes it a counteroffer (UCC § 2-206(1)(b)).

front: When is silence an acceptance?
back: Only if (1) the offeree takes offered services with a reasonable chance to reject and reason to know compensation is expected; (2) the offeror invited silence and the offeree intends to accept; or (3) prior dealings make notice of rejection reasonable. Exercising dominion over goods also counts (R2d § 69).

front: Implied-in-fact contract vs. quasi-contract?
back: An implied-in-fact contract is a real contract shown by conduct. A quasi-contract (implied in law) is a restitution remedy: the reasonable value of a benefit knowingly retained in circumstances making retention unjust; no recovery for volunteers.

front: How definite must a contract be at common law vs. under the UCC?
back: Common law: essential terms reasonably certain, enough to find a breach and give a remedy (R2d § 33). UCC: no failure for indefiniteness if the parties intended to contract and there is a reasonably certain basis for a remedy (§ 2-204(3)); quantity is required.

front: UCC gap fillers: price, place, time, payment?
back: Price: reasonable at the time for delivery (§ 2-305). Place: seller's place of business (§ 2-308). Time: reasonable (§ 2-309). Payment: when and where the buyer receives the goods (§ 2-310).

front: Requirements contract: how much can the buyer demand?
back: Its actual good-faith requirements, but no quantity unreasonably disproportionate to a stated estimate or to normal prior requirements (UCC § 2-306(1)).

front: Define consideration.
back: A performance or return promise that is bargained for: sought by the promisor in exchange for its promise and given by the promisee in exchange for it (R2d § 71). Legal detriment suffices; adequacy is not examined (§ 79).

front: Is a conditional gift promise supported by consideration?
back: No, if the condition is merely a step to receive the gift and was not bargained for (Kirksey v. Kirksey).

front: When is a promise illusory, and how is it cured?
back: When performance is wholly at the promisor's discretion ('as I wish'). It is cured by an implied duty of good faith or reasonable efforts, a notice requirement for termination, or an output/requirements measure (R2d § 77; Wood v. Lucy).

front: State the pre-existing duty rule and its exceptions.
back: Performing a duty already owed to the promisor is not consideration. Exceptions: new or different performance; honest dispute; unanticipated circumstances making the modification fair (R2d § 89); reliance; duty owed to a third party; UCC § 2-209; CA Civ. Code § 1524 (written acceptance of part payment).

front: Is forbearance from suing consideration if the claim is weak?
back: Yes, if the claim is doubtful in fact or law, or the claimant in good faith believes it may be valid (R2d § 74). Not if the claimant knows it is baseless.

front: Is past consideration consideration? What is the material benefit rule?
back: No: nothing was bargained for (Mills v. Wyman). R2d § 86: a promise in recognition of a material benefit previously received is binding to the extent necessary to prevent injustice, unless the benefit was a gift or the promise is disproportionate (Webb v. McGowin).

front: What does Cal. Civ. Code § 1606 say about moral obligation?
back: A moral obligation originating in a benefit conferred on the promisor is good consideration, but courts read it narrowly, usually requiring a prior legal or equitable obligation.

front: State promissory estoppel (R2d § 90).
back: A promise the promisor should reasonably expect to induce action or forbearance, which does induce it, is binding if injustice can be avoided only by enforcement; the remedy may be limited as justice requires (often reliance damages).

front: Common-law rule on modifying a contract?
back: It needs new consideration (pre-existing duty), unless fair and equitable in view of unanticipated circumstances, or enforced because of reliance (R2d § 89). NOM clauses are often treated as waivable.

front: California rule on orally modifying a written contract (Civ. Code § 1698)?
back: A written contract may be modified by a writing; by an oral agreement to the extent executed; or, unless the contract expressly provides otherwise, by an oral agreement supported by new consideration. The SOF applies to the contract as modified.

front: UCC § 2-209 modification rules?
back: No consideration needed, but good faith required. A signed no-oral-modification clause is enforced (on a merchant's form, a non-merchant must sign it separately). The SOF applies if the modified contract is within it. A failed modification may operate as a waiver, retractable absent reliance.

front: Contracts of minors: effect and exceptions?
back: Voidable by the minor, who may disaffirm before majority or within a reasonable time after; ratification after majority ends that power. For necessaries, the minor owes reasonable value (quasi-contract). CA: a minor cannot make a contract relating to real property (Fam. Code § 6701).

front: Tests for mental incapacity (R2d § 15)?
back: Cognitive: unable to understand the nature and consequences of the transaction. Volitional: unable to act reasonably, and the other party has reason to know. Either makes the contract voidable. A person under guardianship has no capacity (void).

front: When does intoxication make a contract voidable?
back: Only if the other party has reason to know that, because of intoxication, the person cannot understand or act reasonably in the transaction (R2d § 16).

front: Elements of duress by improper threat?
back: 1. An improper threat (crime, tort, criminal prosecution, bad-faith civil process, bad-faith threat to breach). 2. No reasonable alternative. 3. Actual inducement. The contract is voidable; physical compulsion makes it void (R2d §§ 174–176).

front: Define undue influence.
back: Unfair persuasion of a party under the persuader's domination, or in a relationship of trust justifying the assumption that the persuader will not act against its welfare; the contract is voidable (R2d § 177; Cal. Civ. Code § 1575).

front: Elements of mutual mistake (R2d § 152)?
back: 1. Both parties mistaken at formation about an existing fact. 2. A basic assumption. 3. A material effect on the exchange. 4. The adversely affected party did not bear the risk (allocated by contract such as 'as is', conscious ignorance, or court allocation).

front: When does a party bear the risk of a mistake (R2d § 154)?
back: (a) The contract allocates it; (b) the party knew its knowledge was limited and treated it as sufficient (conscious ignorance); or (c) the court allocates it as reasonable.

front: Unilateral mistake: what is needed beyond the mutual-mistake elements?
back: Either enforcement would be unconscionable, or the other party had reason to know of the mistake or caused it (R2d § 153; adopted in California in Donovan v. RRL Corp.).

front: Misunderstanding (Raffles v. Wichelhaus): rule?
back: If the parties attach materially different meanings and neither knows or has reason to know the other's meaning, or each does, there is no contract. If only one knows or has reason to know the other's meaning, the contract follows the innocent party's meaning (R2d §§ 20, 201).

front: Elements to rescind for misrepresentation?
back: 1. An assertion not in accord with the facts. 2. Fraudulent or material. 3. Induced assent. 4. Justifiable reliance (R2d § 164). Innocent material misrepresentation suffices; tort damages need scienter.

front: Fraud in the factum vs. fraud in the inducement?
back: In the factum (deception about the nature of the document signed): void. In the inducement (deception about facts motivating assent): voidable.

front: When is nondisclosure treated as a misrepresentation (R2d § 161)?
back: When disclosure is needed to correct a prior assertion; to correct the other party's mistake about a basic assumption where silence breaches good faith; to correct a mistake about a writing's contents; or where a relationship of trust exists. Active concealment always counts.

front: Effect of an illegal contract, and the exceptions?
back: Void and unenforceable by either party (in pari delicto). Exceptions: a party less at fault or protected by the statute; withdrawal before performance; a divisible legal part. Regulatory licensing statutes bar unlicensed parties (CA B&P § 7031); revenue statutes do not.

front: Unconscionability: elements and remedies?
back: Procedural (oppression or surprise) plus substantive (unreasonably one-sided terms), on a sliding scale, judged at formation. The court may refuse to enforce, sever the clause, or limit it (UCC § 2-302; Civ. Code § 1670.5; Armendariz).

front: Noncompete: majority rule vs. California?
back: Majority: enforceable if ancillary to a sale of a business or employment, protecting a legitimate interest, and reasonable in time, place and scope. California: void under B&P § 16600 (Edwards), except narrow statutory exceptions; § 16600.5 (2024) applies regardless of where signed.

front: List the statute of frauds categories (MY LEGS).
back: Marriage (consideration of), Year (cannot be performed within one year), Land (interests; leases over one year), Executor (personal promise to pay estate debts), Goods ($500 or more), Surety (promise to answer for another's debt).

front: What must a SOF memorandum contain?
back: It must reasonably identify the subject matter, show a contract was made, state the essential terms with reasonable certainty, and be signed by the party to be charged. It may be several writings, made later, and electronic (R2d § 131).

front: Sterling v. Taylor (Cal. 2007): role of extrinsic evidence for a SOF memo?
back: Extrinsic evidence may clarify ambiguous essential terms in the memorandum, but it cannot supply essential terms that are missing.

front: How is the SOF one-year provision measured?
back: Ask whether the contract, by its terms, can possibly be fully performed within one year from the date it is made. If yes, however unlikely, it is outside the statute. Lifetime contracts are outside.

front: What is the main purpose (leading object) rule?
back: A promise to pay another's debt is outside the suretyship provision if the promisor's main purpose is to serve its own economic interest.

front: Part performance exception for land contracts?
back: Equity enforces an oral land contract by specific performance where the acts unequivocally refer to the contract, usually two of: possession, payment, substantial improvements; or where there was serious reliance (R2d § 129). California frames this as estoppel (Monarco).

front: UCC § 2-201: what must the writing contain, and what are the exceptions?
back: A writing sufficient to indicate a contract, signed by the defendant, stating a quantity (enforceable only up to that quantity). Exceptions: merchant confirmation without objection in 10 days; specially manufactured goods; admission in court; goods paid for and accepted or received and accepted.

front: Merchant's confirmation rule (§ 2-201(2))?
back: Between merchants, a written confirmation sent within a reasonable time, which the recipient has reason to know of, satisfies the SOF against the recipient unless it objects in writing within 10 days of receipt.

front: Other ways around the SOF?
back: Full performance (one-year provision); promissory estoppel (R2d § 139); admission (UCC); restitution for benefits conferred. Related: equal dignities (Civ. Code § 2309); a modified contract within the SOF must satisfy it (UCC § 2-209(3); Civ. Code § 1698(c)).

front: State the parol evidence rule.
back: If a writing is a final expression (integration), prior agreements and contemporaneous oral agreements cannot contradict it. If it is also complete and exclusive (complete integration), they cannot add consistent terms either. The judge decides integration.

front: When is a consistent additional term admissible against an apparently complete writing?
back: R2d § 216: if agreed for separate consideration, or of a kind that might naturally be omitted from the writing. UCC § 2-202 cmt. 3: unless it would certainly have been included. California (Masterson): unless it would naturally have been included.

front: What purposes does the parol evidence rule NOT bar?
back: Showing whether the writing is integrated; interpreting ambiguity; proving fraud, duress, mistake, illegality or lack of consideration; an oral condition precedent; reformation; a separate agreement with separate consideration; later agreements.

front: What does UCC § 2-202 always let in?
back: Course of dealing, usage of trade and course of performance, to explain or supplement a final writing, unless carefully negated.

front: PG&E v. Thomas Drayage (Cal. 1968) rule?
back: Extrinsic evidence is admissible if relevant to prove a meaning to which the contract language is reasonably susceptible, even if the writing appears unambiguous; the court provisionally receives the evidence to decide that.

front: Riverisland (Cal. 2013) rule?
back: Evidence of fraud is admissible under the parol evidence rule even if it contradicts the terms of the written agreement; it overruled Pendergrass (1935).

front: Main canons of interpretation?
back: Give effect to mutual intent objectively; read as a whole; ordinary meaning; specific over general; negotiated or handwritten over printed; prefer lawful, reasonable, effective meanings; construe ambiguity against the drafter (R2d §§ 202–206; Civ. Code § 1654).

front: Hierarchy of express terms and trade practices (UCC § 1-303)?
back: Express terms > course of performance > course of dealing > usage of trade.

front: What does a court do when an essential term is omitted?
back: It supplies a term reasonable in the circumstances (R2d § 204), e.g., reasonable time, reasonable efforts, a duty to cooperate; it will not contradict an express term.

front: Does an 'as is' clause disclaim the warranty of title?
back: No. Title may be excluded only by specific language or circumstances showing the seller does not claim title (UCC § 2-312(2)).

front: How is an express warranty created?
back: By an affirmation of fact or promise, a description, or a sample or model that becomes part of the basis of the bargain; no formal words needed; puffery and opinion excluded (UCC § 2-313).

front: Implied warranty of merchantability: who gives it and what does it require?
back: A merchant seller of goods of that kind. The goods must be fit for their ordinary purposes, pass without objection in the trade, and be adequately packaged and labeled (UCC § 2-314).

front: Implied warranty of fitness for a particular purpose: elements?
back: The seller (any seller) has reason to know at contracting of the buyer's particular purpose and of the buyer's reliance on the seller's skill or judgment; the buyer actually relies (UCC § 2-315).

front: How do you disclaim implied warranties?
back: Merchantability: mention 'merchantability'; if written, conspicuous. Fitness: a conspicuous writing. Or 'as is' / 'with all faults', or the buyer's examination. A disclaimer inconsistent with an express warranty is inoperative (UCC § 2-316).

front: Warranty claim: notice and limitations rules?
back: An accepting buyer must notify the seller within a reasonable time after discovering the breach or be barred (UCC § 2-607(3)(a)). Suit within 4 years of tender of delivery, reducible to 1 year (§ 2-725).

front: Express condition: standard of compliance?
back: Strict (literal) compliance; substantial performance is not enough. In doubtful cases courts read the language as a promise, to avoid forfeiture (R2d § 227).

front: Satisfaction clauses: which test applies?
back: Personal taste or fancy: subjective, honest good-faith dissatisfaction. Commercial value or mechanical fitness: objective, reasonable-person test.

front: Constructive conditions: order of performance defaults?
back: If performances can be simultaneous, they are concurrent conditions, and a party must tender to put the other in breach. If one takes time (work), it comes before the one that does not (payment) (R2d § 234).

front: How can the non-occurrence of a condition be excused?
back: Waiver; estoppel; wrongful prevention or hindrance; repudiation; impossibility of a non-material condition; disproportionate forfeiture where the condition was not a material part of the exchange (R2d § 229).

front: Substantial performance: rule and limits?
back: A party that substantially performed recovers the contract price less damages for defects (Jacob & Youngs). It does not apply to express conditions or sales of goods, and a willful deviation weighs against it.

front: Factors for material breach (R2d § 241)?
back: (a) Extent of deprivation of the expected benefit; (b) adequacy of damages; (c) forfeiture by the breaching party; (d) likelihood of cure; (e) the breaching party's good faith.

front: Effects of material vs. minor breach?
back: Material: the injured party may suspend performance and, if not cured, terminate and sue for total breach. Minor: damages only; the injured party must keep performing, and terminating would itself be a material breach.

front: When is time of the essence?
back: When the contract says so expressly, or the circumstances make timing vital (perishables, seasonal goods, a known deadline). Otherwise delay is usually a minor breach.

front: Divisible contract rule?
back: If performances can be apportioned into pairs of agreed equivalents, a party recovers for each completed part even if it breaches another part, less damages (R2d § 240).

front: What counts as anticipatory repudiation?
back: A clear, unequivocal statement, or a voluntary act, before performance is due, showing a party will not or cannot perform (R2d § 250; UCC § 2-610). Doubts or requests to renegotiate are not enough.

front: Options of the non-repudiating party?
back: Treat it as a total breach and sue at once; suspend and await performance for a commercially reasonable time; or urge retraction. It must mitigate and may not keep performing to increase damages.

front: Until when can a repudiation be retracted?
back: Until the repudiator's next performance is due, unless the aggrieved party has cancelled, materially changed position, or indicated the repudiation is final (including by suing) (R2d § 256; UCC § 2-611).

front: Adequate assurance under UCC § 2-609?
back: On reasonable grounds for insecurity, a party may demand adequate assurance in writing and suspend performance; failure to provide it within a reasonable time, not exceeding 30 days, is a repudiation.

front: Define good faith under the UCC, and state its limit.
back: Honesty in fact and observance of reasonable commercial standards of fair dealing (UCC § 1-201(b)(20)). The implied covenant (R2d § 205) cannot override express terms (Carma).

front: Perfect tender rule (§ 2-601)?
back: If goods or the tender fail in any respect to conform, the buyer may reject all, accept all, or accept any commercial units and reject the rest. Limits: cure, installment contracts, agreed remedy limits, good faith.

front: Procedure for an effective rejection?
back: Within a reasonable time after delivery, with seasonable notice to the seller, particularizing curable defects; then hold the goods with reasonable care for the seller and do not use them as owner (UCC §§ 2-602, 2-605).

front: Seller's right to cure (§ 2-508)?
back: If time remains, the seller may notify and deliver conforming goods by the deadline. After the deadline, only if it reasonably believed the tender would be acceptable, with seasonable notice and within a further reasonable time.

front: How does a buyer accept goods (§ 2-606)?
back: By signifying acceptance after a reasonable opportunity to inspect, failing to make an effective rejection, or doing an act inconsistent with the seller's ownership.

front: Elements of revocation of acceptance (§ 2-608)?
back: A nonconformity substantially impairing value to the buyer; acceptance on a reasonable assumption of cure that did not occur, or without discovery (latent defect or seller's assurances); within a reasonable time; before substantial change; notice to the seller.

front: Installment contracts (§ 2-612)?
back: The buyer may reject an installment only if its nonconformity substantially impairs that installment's value and cannot be cured. The whole contract is breached only if the default substantially impairs the value of the whole contract.

front: F.O.B. seller's city vs. F.O.B. buyer's city?
back: F.O.B. seller's city = shipment contract (risk passes on due delivery to the carrier). F.O.B. buyer's city = destination contract (risk passes on tender at the destination). Carriage without a term is presumed to be a shipment contract.

front: Risk of loss absent breach: the order of analysis?
back: Agreement → shipment contract (on delivery to carrier) / destination contract (on tender there) → bailee (document or acknowledgment) → otherwise merchant seller: on the buyer's receipt; non-merchant seller: on tender (UCC § 2-509).

front: Risk of loss where the seller's tender is nonconforming?
back: Risk stays on the seller until cure or acceptance (UCC § 2-510(1)), even under a shipment contract.

front: Risk of loss where the buyer repudiates after goods are identified?
back: The seller may treat the risk as on the buyer for a commercially reasonable time, to the extent the seller's insurance is deficient (UCC § 2-510(3)).

front: Casualty to identified goods (§ 2-613)?
back: If goods identified when the contract was made are destroyed without fault before risk passes, the contract is avoided (total loss). For partial loss, the buyer may avoid or accept with a price allowance.

front: Voidable title and entrustment (§ 2-403)?
back: A person with voidable title (fraud, bad check) can pass good title to a good-faith purchaser for value. Entrusting goods to a merchant who deals in such goods lets the merchant pass the entruster's rights to a buyer in the ordinary course. A thief passes no title.

front: Impossibility: elements and classic triggers?
back: A supervening event; objective impossibility; non-occurrence was a basic assumption; no fault; risk not assumed. Triggers: destruction of the specific subject matter, death or incapacity of a necessary person, supervening illegality (Taylor v. Caldwell).

front: Impracticability: standard and UCC rule?
back: Performance possible only at excessive and unreasonable cost or difficulty, due to an unforeseen event whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption; no fault; risk not assumed. A price rise alone is not enough. UCC § 2-615: allocate fairly and notify.

front: Frustration of purpose: elements?
back: A principal purpose, known to both parties, is substantially frustrated by a supervening event whose non-occurrence was a basic assumption; no fault; risk not allocated (R2d § 265; Krell v. Henry). Applied narrowly (Lloyd v. Murphy).

front: Mutual rescission: requirements?
back: Mutual agreement while both sides have executory duties (each surrender is consideration). Oral is fine unless the SOF or a § 2-209(2) clause requires a writing. It cannot defeat vested third-party beneficiary rights.

front: California Civ. Code § 1542?
back: A general release does not extend to claims the releasing party does not know or suspect to exist in its favor when signing, if knowing them would have materially affected the settlement, unless that protection is waived.

front: Executory accord vs. substituted contract?
back: An executory accord suspends the original duty until satisfaction; if the debtor breaches the accord, the creditor may sue on either. A substituted contract discharges the original duty immediately.

front: Full-payment check rule (UCC § 3-311)?
back: If a claim is unliquidated or disputed, and the debtor in good faith tenders a check with a conspicuous full-satisfaction statement, the claimant who obtains payment discharges the claim (subject to statutory exceptions).

front: What is a novation?
back: A substituted contract that adds a new party, usually a new obligor replacing the original one with the obligee's consent, releasing the original obligor (R2d § 280).

front: Expectation damages formula (R2d § 347)?
back: Loss in value of the other party's performance + incidental + consequential damages − cost avoided − loss avoided. Goal: the position full performance would have produced.

front: Owner's damages when a builder breaches?
back: The reasonable cost of completion or repair, unless clearly disproportionate to the value added (economic waste); then the diminution in market value (Groves; Peevyhouse; Jacob & Youngs).

front: Builder's damages when the owner breaches mid-performance?
back: Expected profit + costs incurred − payments received (= contract price − cost saved by not finishing − payments). It cannot recover for work done after the repudiation.

front: Wrongfully discharged employee's damages?
back: Salary for the remaining term minus what the employee earned, or could have earned with reasonable effort, in substantially similar employment; no duty to take a different or inferior job (Parker v. Twentieth Century-Fox).

front: Hadley v. Baxendale: rule for consequential damages?
back: Recoverable only if, at contracting, the loss either arises naturally in the ordinary course from the breach, or results from special circumstances the breaching party had reason to know (R2d § 351; UCC § 2-715(2); Civ. Code § 3300).

front: Can a seller recover consequential damages under Article 2?
back: No. A seller gets incidental damages (§ 2-710) and its price, resale, market or lost-profit measure, but not consequential damages.

front: Certainty rule for lost profits?
back: Damages must be proved with reasonable certainty. An established business can use its history. A new business's lost profits were traditionally barred, and now need reasonably certain proof; otherwise fall back to reliance damages (R2d § 352).

front: What are incidental damages?
back: Reasonable costs of responding to the breach: inspection, transport, storage and care of rejected goods, costs of cover or resale (UCC §§ 2-710, 2-715(1)).

front: Duty to mitigate: rule and limits?
back: No recovery for losses avoidable by reasonable effort without undue risk or burden; reasonable mitigation costs are recoverable; the breaching party bears the burden. Employees need not take inferior jobs; a lost-volume seller's resale does not reduce damages (R2d § 350).

front: Liquidated damages vs. penalty: test?
back: Enforceable if the amount is reasonable in light of the anticipated or actual loss and the difficulty of proof (R2d § 356; UCC § 2-718(1)); traditional test: damages hard to estimate + reasonable forecast. Otherwise it is a penalty, and actual damages apply.

front: California liquidated damages rule (Civ. Code § 1671)?
back: In most contracts a clause is presumed valid unless the challenger proves it was unreasonable under the circumstances when made (§ 1671(b)). In specified consumer contracts and residential leases it is void unless actual damages would be impracticable or extremely difficult to fix.

front: UCC § 2-719: exclusive remedies and failure of essential purpose?
back: Parties may limit remedies (e.g., repair or replace), exclusive only if expressly agreed. If the limited remedy fails of its essential purpose, general Code remedies apply. Consequential-damages exclusions are valid unless unconscionable (personal injury, consumer goods: prima facie unconscionable).

front: Punitive and emotional-distress damages for breach?
back: Punitive: not recoverable unless the conduct is also a tort (R2d § 355; Civ. Code § 3294). Emotional distress: not recoverable unless bodily harm, or the contract makes serious distress particularly likely (R2d § 353; Erlich v. Menezes).

front: Seller's UCC damages when the buyer breaches?
back: Contract price − resale price (§ 2-706), or contract price − market price at the time and place of tender (§ 2-708(1)), plus incidental damages (§ 2-710), minus expenses saved; lost-volume profit (§ 2-708(2)); or the price (§ 2-709).

front: Who is a lost-volume seller, and what does it recover?
back: A seller with enough supply to make both the breached sale and the resale; it recovers its lost profit, including reasonable overhead, plus incidental damages (UCC § 2-708(2); Neri).

front: When can a seller sue for the price (§ 2-709)?
back: For goods accepted; for conforming goods lost or damaged after risk passed to the buyer; or for identified goods the seller cannot reasonably resell (e.g., custom goods).

front: Buyer's UCC damages when the seller fails to deliver or the buyer rightfully rejects?
back: Cover price − contract price (§ 2-712), or market price when the buyer learned of the breach − contract price (§ 2-713), plus incidental and consequential damages, minus expenses saved, plus a refund of the price paid.

front: Buyer's damages for accepted nonconforming goods (§ 2-714)?
back: For breach of warranty: value as warranted − value as accepted, measured at the time and place of acceptance, plus incidental and consequential damages; the buyer may deduct these from the price due (§ 2-717).

front: Elements of specific performance (CCIFD)?
back: Contract with definite terms; Conditions satisfied (plaintiff ready, willing, able); Inadequate legal remedy (land, unique goods); Feasibility (no personal services, manageable supervision); no Defenses (laches, unclean hands, unconscionability, BFP).

front: Can a court order specific performance of a personal-services contract?
back: No. At most, a negative injunction barring a person with unique skills from working for a competitor during the term, if reasonable (Lumley v. Wagner). California allows it only under Civ. Code § 3423(e).

front: California Civ. Code § 3387?
back: Breach of an agreement to transfer real property is presumed not adequately relieved by money damages; the presumption is conclusive for a single-family dwelling the buyer intends to occupy.

front: Requirements for rescission as a remedy?
back: A ground (misrepresentation, mistake, duress, undue influence, incapacity, material breach, agreement); prompt action and notice; restoration or an offer to restore what was received (Civ. Code § 1691). Barred by affirmation, unreasonable delay, or third-party rights. CA § 1692: damages may accompany rescission.

front: When is reformation available?
back: When a writing fails to express the actual agreement because of mutual mistake in expression, or fraud or a known unilateral mistake. Not barred by the parol evidence rule, the SOF or negligence; barred by a bona fide purchaser and laches.

front: Reliance damages: measure and limit?
back: Expenditures in preparation or performance, minus any loss the breaching party proves the plaintiff would have suffered on a losing contract (R2d § 349). Used for uncertain profits and promissory estoppel.

front: Restitution for the non-breaching party: measure and limit?
back: The reasonable value of the benefit conferred, or the increase in the defendant's wealth (R2d § 371). Not available if the injured party has fully performed and only a definite money debt remains (§ 373(2)).

front: Breaching party's restitution: rule and UCC deposit formula?
back: Benefit conferred minus the injured party's damages (R2d § 374; Britton v. Turner). UCC § 2-718(2): absent a valid LD clause, the seller keeps the lesser of 20% of the price or $500, subject to offset for proven damages.

front: Intended vs. incidental beneficiary?
back: Intended (creditor or donee): the parties intended the third party to benefit, so it may enforce (R2d § 302). Incidental: only an indirect benefit, so no rights.

front: California's third-party beneficiary test (Goonewardene)?
back: (1) The third party would in fact benefit; (2) a motivating purpose of the contracting parties was to benefit it; (3) letting it sue is consistent with the contract's objectives and the parties' reasonable expectations.

front: When do a beneficiary's rights vest?
back: When it manifests assent at a party's request, sues on the promise, or materially changes position in justifiable reliance (R2d § 311). Before vesting, the parties may modify or rescind without its consent.

front: Which defenses can a promisor raise against a beneficiary?
back: Any defense arising from the contract that it could raise against the promisee (fraud, failure of consideration, non-occurrence of a condition), but not its claims or defenses against the promisee that arise outside the contract, such as set-off of an unrelated debt (R2d § 309).

front: Which contract rights are not assignable?
back: Rights whose assignment would materially change the obligor's duty, increase its burden or risk, or impair return performance (e.g., personal services); those forbidden by law; those validly precluded by contract (R2d § 317).

front: Effect of an anti-assignment clause?
back: A ban on assigning 'the contract' bars only delegation. A ban on assigning rights gives a damages claim but does not void the assignment unless it says assignments are void. Clauses restricting assignment of payment rights are ineffective (UCC § 9-406(d)).

front: Obligor pays the assignor before getting notice of the assignment. Result?
back: The obligor is discharged; the assignee must recover from the assignor (R2d § 338). After notice, only payment to the assignee discharges.

front: Successive assignments of the same right: who wins?
back: Majority: the first assignee, unless a later assignee for value without notice first obtains payment, a judgment, a novation or a delivered token (R2d § 342). Minority (English): the first to notify the obligor.

front: Delegation: limits and liability?
back: Duties are delegable unless personal (skill, trust), prohibited by contract, or barred by law. The delegator remains liable unless there is a novation; the delegate is liable to the obligee only if it assumes the duty.

front: Rattagan v. Uber (Cal. 2024): rule?
back: A contracting party may sue in tort for fraudulent concealment during performance if the tort's elements exist independently of the contract and the conduct exposes it to a risk of harm beyond what the parties contemplated.

front: Key UCC numbers: SOF, firm offer, confirmation objection, assurance, deposit, limitations?
back: $500 (§ 2-201); 3 months (§ 2-205); 10 days to object to a merchant confirmation (§ 2-201(2)); 30 days to give adequate assurance (§ 2-609); lesser of 20% or $500 (§ 2-718(2)); 4 years, reducible to 1 (§ 2-725).
